paras: The lynching of Frank Craft, William Underwood and James Butler took place on the night of July 1, 1881, when a mob took the three men from the jail at Greenfield, Dade County, Missouri, and hanged them in the court-yard. The men were jailed as horse thieves and described as members of a gang led by Taylor Underwood, who was accused of killing the Greenfield officer McElrath. The hanging was reported in brief items across the country in July and was recalled in August when Taylor Underwood was arrested at Carthage.

According to an 1882 Sedalia account, McElrath, the city marshal of Greenfield, was shot on June 20, 1881 in a saloon after telling Taylor Underwood that he had to arrest him, and Underwood escaped on a cut-loose horse. A Springfield dispatch to the St. Louis Globe-Democrat said that public feeling against the gang of horse thieves to which Underwood belonged then "culminated" in the lynching. Members of the gang still at large were the object of "a vigorous search" at the time.

Late on the night of July 1, a mob went to the house of Sheriff Whiteside, bound him, and took the keys to the jail. The men then took Craft, Underwood and Butler from the jail into the court-yard and "hanged them to trees until life was extinct." A shorter wire version described the party as "about 50 disguised men" who hanged the three to a tree in the jail-yard, and another note called them "masked men."

A fourth prisoner, Mitchell, was left in his cell, the dispatch said, because the mob thought he would be needed as a witness against the rest of the gang. That decision gave rise to an early report, later corrected, that Mitchell had escaped from the mob.

No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage. Taylor Underwood was arrested at Carthage on August 5, 1881 after a struggle with Detective E. S. Pike, and the wire on his capture said three of his gang had been lynched by Dade county citizens "for being concerned in the murder of McElrath." Tried in Barton County on a change of venue, he was sentenced to hang in December 1881, won a rehearing, and in 1882 received ninety-nine years in the penitentiary.

In a jail interview at Lamar, Underwood said that his brother Jasper, who helped bring about his arrest, had a son "taken out of the Greenfield jail" and hanged by a mob, though he did not give the son's name. In a later narrative he said the son had been hanged for horse stealing.

White newspapers covered the lynching mostly in one-sentence entries in news summaries from Pennsylvania to Arkansas and Georgia. The Chicago Tribune printed the fullest account under "Criminal News" and a "Lynch Law" heading, saying the "miscreants" had been summoned "to the bar of Judge Lynch." None of the reports gave the race of the victims or commented on the mob, and all described the dead as horse thieves and desperadoes.

In August the St. Louis Republican's Carthage special on Underwood's capture carried the lynching as a closing sentence, which ran under such headings as "Important Capture" and "Lynching Desperadoes." The Somerset Herald wrote that the three had been lynched "for supposed connection" with the murder, while the Eaton Democrat misread the wire and reported that Taylor Underwood himself "was lynched at Carthage."

The brief July items placed the lynching at "Springfield, Dade county," while the fuller dispatch, datelined Springfield, attributed the news to "advices from Greenfield" and placed the jail there. Accounts also differ on McElrath's office, calling him deputy sheriff, marshal or city marshal, and on when he was killed, from "a few days" before the lynching to "three months" before August.

A mob of about fifty bound the sheriff, took three prisoners described as horse thieves from the jail and hanged them, which the dispatch called summoning them 'to the bar of Judge Lynch' (A2, A3, A9); the August wire says they were lynched for being concerned in the murder of an officer (A17).

Two separate July wire versions (the Globe-Democrat dispatch in A3/A9 and the 'about fifty disguised men' version in A2/A4) agree on the three names and the hanging at the jail, and the August Carthage wire refers back to it (A17, A22).

The 1882 trial reports call him city marshal of Greenfield.
